The first step is the product rule for a scalar function times a vector function (Stewart §13.2, Theorem 3, rule 3). The two “since” lines use last week’s formulas: (§13.3, Equation 9) and the definition (§13.3). So the board has shown the result of Stewart §13.4, Equation 7: . In words: the tangential part is how fast the speed changes; the normal part is how sharply the path bends times speed squared (that’s why you are pushed sideways harder on a tight curve taken fast).

4Ch. 14 Partial Derivatives · 14.1 Functions of Several Variables

New chapter. Two photos of the same board: one while it was being written, one finished.

Board headings: Ch. 14: Partial Derivatives  ·  14.1 Functions of Several Variables.

Definition

A function of two (or more) variables is a rule that assigns to every ordered pair (or ) in some domain a unique real number, denoted (or ).

The range of is the set of all values for in .

Explanation (added)

“Unique” is the key word: each input pair gets exactly one output. This is the same idea as from first-year calculus, except the input is now a point of the plane (two numbers), not a single number. Stewart §14.1 opens with the same definition under “Functions of Two Variables”.

Explanation (added)

One input number plus one output number gives a point in the plane, so the graph of is a curve in . Two input numbers plus one output gives a point in space, so the graph of is a surface in : above each in the domain sits the point at height . Explanation (added)

Squaring turns the function into the full sphere from 12.1, but the square root never gives a negative , so the graph is only the top half. That also gives the range: the largest output is at the centre, ; the smallest is 0, on the edge circle. Each trace is a circle centred on the -axis whose radius shrinks as you go up; stacking them up builds the dome. Check: gives radius 4 (the domain’s edge) and gives radius 0 ✓.

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Given , find the tangential and normal components and of the acceleration (two derivatives, one dot product, one cross product). Test 2 material, not Test 1.
  • For a given , evaluate it at a point, then find and sketch the domain: shade the allowed region, solid boundary if included, dashed if not.
  • Find the domain and range of something like or , written in set or interval notation.
  • Sketch the graph of a linear function such as from its three intercepts.
  • Sketch using traces : identify each trace (circle, ellipse, point) and name the surface.
